hook: The labourer's son who became the Prince of Mathematicians, and found a lost planet with pen and paper.

pages.t: A boy who counted before he talked
pages.x: Carl Friedrich Gauss was born in Brunswick, in northern Germany, in 1777. His father did hard jobs as a gardener, bricklayer and canal hand; his mother could not read. The family told how, aged three, he watched his father add up the wages of his workmen and quietly pointed out a mistake. He was right.

The story goes that when he was about nine, his teacher kept the class busy by telling them to add up every number from 1 to 100. Gauss wrote one number on his slate at once: 5050. He had seen that 1 + 100, 2 + 99, 3 + 98 and so on make 50 pairs of 101. The teacher bought him a better maths book, and soon the Duke of Brunswick paid for his schooling.

On 30 March 1796, a student of 18 at Göttingen, he proved that a regular polygon with 17 sides can be drawn with only a ruler and compass. Nobody had found a new one since the ancient Greeks, 2,000 years before. That day he chose mathematics over languages, and began a diary of his discoveries.

In 1801, aged 24, he published his book on whole numbers. It set out "clock arithmetic", where 10 + 5 makes 3 on a twelve-hour clock, proved laws about primes that Euler had only guessed, and turned scattered puzzles into a science.
pages.fx: It founded modern number theory. The same mathematics of primes and remainders now keeps bank cards, online payments and messages secret.

pages.x: On 1 January 1801 an Italian astronomer found Ceres, a small new world between Mars and Jupiter, then lost it in the Sun's glare after 41 days. With so few sightings no one could say where it had gone. Gauss invented a new way to work out its path. On 31 December it was found again, almost exactly where he said. He was famous at 24.

A French mathematician wrote him brilliant letters as "Monsieur Le Blanc". In 1806, when Napoleon's army took Brunswick, the writer, afraid he would die like Archimedes, asked a French general to keep him safe. So Gauss learned the truth: Le Blanc was Sophie Germain, a woman who had had to teach herself. He praised her "noblest courage".

In 1807 he became director of the new observatory at Göttingen, and stayed for the rest of his life, 48 years. Two years later his beloved wife Johanna died after the birth of their third child, and the baby soon followed. He wrote that he could hardly bear it. In 1810 he married her friend Minna Waldeck.
pages.cap: The observatory he ran for 48 years

pages.x: In 1809 he showed how to get the truest answer from many measurements that are each a little wrong: the errors mostly fall on a bell-shaped curve, and the best fit is the one that makes the squares of the errors smallest.
pages.fx: The "Gaussian" bell curve now runs through science: heights, exam scores, factory checks, the margin of error of every opinion poll, and the fitting of data that machine learning is built on.

pages.x: From 1818 he surveyed the Kingdom of Hanover, often in the field himself. To sight distant hilltops he invented the heliotrope, a mirror that flashes sunlight for many kilometres. The work led him to a new geometry of curved surfaces.
pages.fx: He found that a surface's curve can be measured from within it. His student Riemann took this further, and Einstein used it to describe gravity as curved space and time.

pages.x: In 1833 he and the young physicist Wilhelm Weber ran a wire over the roofs of Göttingen, about a kilometre from the observatory to the physics laboratory, and sent each other messages by pulses of electric current that swung a magnetic needle.
pages.fx: It was one of the first electric telegraphs: within 40 years, wires crossed the continents and the oceans. Their study of the Earth's magnetism gave a unit its name, the gauss.

pages.x: His motto was "pauca sed matura", few but ripe: he published only what was perfect. A strange new geometry, where the angles of a triangle add up to less than 180 degrees, stayed in his drawer until younger men found it. He died in Göttingen in 1855, aged 77. His brain was kept for science, and in 2013 it turned out it had been swapped with another man's.
pages.cap: A triangle on a saddle, its angles under 180 degrees

pages.x: Gauss changed almost every part of mathematics and physics: numbers, statistics, geometry, astronomy and magnetism. He is remembered as the Prince of Mathematicians, and for years his face and his bell curve were on Germany's 10-mark note.
pts: Found the lost planet Ceres with new mathematics
Gave us the bell curve and the method of least squares
Built one of the first electric telegraphs
